blocks.text: The angle theta that specifies the instantaneous value of an alternating voltage or current is called its phase. With V = Vo sin(wt) = Vo sin(theta) and I = Io sin(wt) = Io sin(theta), the points A, B, C, D and E of one cycle have phases 0, pi/2, pi, 3 pi/2 and 2 pi (Fig 17.5 a): each point of an AC cycle corresponds to a phase.

blocks.alt: One green cycle of alternating voltage between +Vo and -Vo. Points A, B, C, D and E on the axis theta = omega t are at phases 0, pi/2, pi, 3 pi/2 and 2 pi.
blocks.caption: Figure 17.5 (a): AC cycle corresponds to a phase (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 17.5 (a)).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 17.5(a) labels the axis '2 theta = wt'; it is theta = wt, as the text says and as drawn above.

The value of theta at t = 0 is the initial phase. With V = Vo sin(theta) and I = Io sin(theta) (17.9), voltage and current both have initial phase zero and are in phase. Often they are not. If V = Vo sin(theta) and I = Io sin(theta + phi), then at t = 0 the voltage is zero but the current is already positive (Io sin phi): the current reached zero earlier, by an angle phi, so the current leads the voltage by phi (Fig 17.5 b). If I = Io sin(theta - phi), the current reaches zero later, by phi, and lags behind the voltage (Fig 17.5 c). The angle phi is the phase difference between V and I.

blocks.alt: Two graphs against t. (b) Positive phase: the red current I = Io sin(theta + phi) starts a distance phi before t = 0, has the value Io sin phi at t = 0 and peaks at +Io before the green voltage V. (c) Negative phase: the current I = Io sin(theta - phi) has the value -Io sin phi at t = 0 and crosses zero phi after V.
blocks.caption: Figure 17.5 (b), (c): Graphical representation showing (b) current leads the voltage, (c) current lags behind voltage (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 17.5 (b), (c)).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figures 17.5(b) and (c) give the values at t = 0 as 'Io sin theta'. At t = 0 they are Io sin phi and -Io sin phi, as drawn above.

items: The length of the rotating vector represents, on some scale, the peak or rms value of the alternating quantity.
The vector is horizontal at the instant when the quantity is zero and increasing positively.
The vector rotates anticlockwise with the same angular frequency as the alternating quantity.

blocks.text: Fig 17.5 (d) shows a voltage waveform leading the current waveform by 90 degrees (pi/2 rad). In Fig 17.5 (e), vector OI represents the current, taken as the reference, and OV represents the voltage, leading by 90 degrees; both vectors rotate anticlockwise at the angular frequency.

blocks.alt: (d) The red voltage V and the green current I against time; V reaches its peak a quarter cycle, pi/2, before I. (e) Vector diagram from O: OI horizontal labelled current and OV vertical labelled voltage, with a 90 degree mark between them.
blocks.caption: Figure 17.5 (d), (e): (d) Graphical representation showing voltage V leads current I by pi/2; (e) vector diagram OI and OV showing V leads I by 90 degrees or pi/2 rad (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 17.5 (d), (e)).
